title: Λόχος καὶ γόος
titleEn: The Ambush Plot and Penelope's Grief — Odyssey 4.641–741
part: The Ambush Plot and Penelope's Grief (4.641–741)
about: Antinous questions Noemon about who sailed with Telemachus, and learns that a leader who looked like Mentor — or perhaps a god wearing his shape — led the chosen young men aboard. Alarmed, the suitors abandon their games to confer, and Antinous proposes waylaying Telemachus's ship in the strait between Ithaca and Same to kill him on his way home. The herald Medon, who has overheard the plot, hurries to warn Penelope, who reproaches him and the suitors bitterly for their cruelty and their waste of her household. Overcome with grief once Medon confirms that her son's life is in danger, Penelope collapses in tears among her serving-women, rebukes them for not waking her when Telemachus set sail, and resolves to send for the old servant Dolios so that he may carry word of it all to Laertes.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος προσέφη Ἐυπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is the house-fixed reply-formula τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος προσέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός, here spelled Ἐυ- rather than the contracted Εὐ-: the edition keeps ἐύ- and ἐυ- without a printed diaeresis, as elsewhere. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι 'speak to, address'.

sentences.t:
νημερτές μοι ἔνισπε, πότ’ ᾤχετο καὶ τίνες αὐτῷ
κοῦροι ἕποντ’;
sentences.l:
“Truly to me tell, when he went, and who with him
young men followed?
sentences.i: “Tell me truly — when did he set out, and what young men went with him?
sentences.n: νημερτές, neuter accusative used adverbially, 'truly, unerringly' (from νη- 'not' + the root of ἁμαρτάνω 'miss the mark', as in νημερτής 'unerring' of Proteus). ἔνισπε is an aorist imperative of ἐνέπω 'tell, relate'. πότ’ is πότε, elided. ᾤχετο is the augmented imperfect of οἴχομαι 'be gone, have gone' (οἰ- lengthened to ᾠ-). ἕποντ’ is ἕποντο, imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow, accompany', here 'were accompanying him'.

sentences.t:
Ἰθάκης ἐξαίρετοι, ἦ ἑοὶ αὐτοῦ
θῆτές τε δμῶές τε;
sentences.l:
Chosen men of Ithaca, or his own
hired men and slaves?
sentences.i: Chosen men of Ithaca, or his own hired hands and household slaves?
sentences.n: ἐξαίρετοι, 'picked out, choice', a verbal adjective from ἐξαιρέομαι 'choose out'. ἑοί is the possessive ὅς, ἥ, ὅν, 'his own', not the article; αὐτοῦ here is the adverb 'there, at home' rather than the pronoun. θῆτες are hired labourers, free men who work for wages, distinct from δμῶες, household slaves.

sentences.t: δύναιτό κε καὶ τὸ τελέσσαι.
sentences.l: This too he might be able to accomplish.
sentences.i: That much, at least, he could manage on his own.
sentences.n: δύναιτό is the present optative of δύναμαι with κε, a potential statement: 'he could'. τό is the pronoun, 'this', object of τελέσσαι, the uncontracted aorist infinitive of τελέω 'bring to pass, accomplish'.

sentences.t:
καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐὺ εἰδῶ,
ἤ σε βίῃ ἀέκοντος ἀπηύρα νῆα μέλαιναν,
ἦε ἑκών οἱ δῶκας, ἐπεὶ προσπτύξατο μύθῳ.
sentences.l:
And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well,
whether he took away your black ship by force, against your will,
or you gave it to him willingly, since he pleaded with you in words.”
sentences.i: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well: whether he took your black ship away by force, against your will, or you gave it to him willingly, when he pleaded with you.”
sentences.n: Line 645 repeats a line already published in odyssey-002, whose 'l' and 'i' are kept for that line; the sentence then goes its own way. ἀπηύρα is an unaugmented aorist of ἀπαυράω 'take away, rob', with an ending that looks like an imperfect. προσπτύξατο, aorist middle of προσπτύσσομαι, is literally 'folded himself toward', hence 'clasped, entreated'; μύθῳ is the instrumental dative, 'with a word, with a plea'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ υἱὸς Φρονίοιο Νοήμων ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: Him then the son of Phronius, Noemon, addressed, face to face:
sentences.i: Then Noemon, son of Phronius, spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A new reply-formula: unlike the fixed τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ [Name] [patronymic] ἀντίον ηὔδα pattern, here the patronymic periphrasis υἱὸς Φρονίοιο, 'the son of Phronius', stands before the name itself, and αὖ is absent. Recorded in new-renderings.md. Φρονίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου). ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak, say', augmented (αὐ- → ηὐ-).

sentences.t: αὐτὸς ἑκών οἱ δῶκα·
sentences.l: “I myself gave it to him willingly;
sentences.i: “I gave it to him myself, and willingly;
sentences.n: αὐτός is emphatic, 'I myself'; ἑκών, 'willing', answers Antinous's alternative ἀέκοντος at 4.646. δῶκα is an unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι (= ἔδωκα).

sentences.l:
What would even another have done,
whenever such a man, having cares upon his heart,
asks for one?
sentences.i: What would anyone else have done, when a man like that, with such cares on his heart, comes asking?
sentences.n: τί κεν ῥέξειε is a potential optative, 'what would he have done'. ὁππότ’ = ὁπότε, epic (Attic ὁπότε). αἰτίζῃ is a present subjunctive (indefinite 'whenever'), from αἰτίζω 'ask, beg'.

sentences.t: χαλεπόν κεν ἀνήνασθαι δόσιν εἴη.
sentences.l: Hard would it have been to refuse the gift.
sentences.i: It would have been hard to refuse the gift.
sentences.n: χαλεπόν κεν ... εἴη is a potential optative with an impersonal adjective, 'it would be hard'; ἀνήνασθαι, aorist middle infinitive of ἀναίνομαι, is 'to refuse, deny'.

sentences.t:
κοῦροι δ’, οἳ κατὰ δῆμον ἀριστεύουσι μεθ’ ἡμέας,
οἵ οἱ ἕποντ’·
sentences.l:
But the young men who throughout the district are foremost among us,
these followed him;
sentences.i: But the young men who are foremost in the land among us — these are the ones who went with him;
sentences.n: ἀριστεύουσι is 'are best, excel', from ἄριστος. μεθ’ ἡμέας is μετά + accusative, 'among us'. οἵ οἱ ἕποντ’ resumes the relative clause with a further pronoun, 'these, they followed him' — a common epic pattern of picking the subject back up.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἀρχὸν ἐγὼ βαίνοντ’ ἐνόησα
Μέντορα, ἠὲ θεόν, τῷ δ’ αὐτῷ πάντα ἐῴκει.
sentences.l:
and I noticed their leader stepping aboard,
Mentor, or a god — in everything he was like the man himself.
sentences.i: and I noticed their leader stepping aboard — Mentor, or a god who was like him in every way.
sentences.n: ἐν ... ἐνόησα is tmesis for ἐνενόησα, 'I noticed, observed'. βαίνοντ’ is a present participle, 'stepping, boarding'. ἐῴκει is the pluperfect-with-imperfect-force of ἔοικα 'be like'; τῷ δ’ αὐτῷ is 'to that very man', i.e. to Mentor. The doubt Noemon voices — Mentor, or a god who looked exactly like him — signals to the audience, though not to the suitors, that this was Athena in disguise.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ τὸ θαυμάζω·
sentences.l: But this I marvel at:
sentences.i: But here is the thing that puzzles me:
sentences.n: τό is the pronoun, object of θαυμάζω, anticipating the fact stated in the next clause.

sentences.t:
ἴδον ἐνθάδε Μέντορα δῖον
χθιζὸν ὑπηοῖον, τότε δ’ ἔμβη νηὶ Πύλονδε.
sentences.l:
I saw heavenly Mentor here
yesterday, at dawn — but then he had already embarked, by ship, for Pylos.”
sentences.i: I saw heavenly Mentor here just yesterday morning, and yet he had already sailed for Pylos.”
sentences.n: ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω (= εἶδον). δῖον here keeps the table's fixed 'heavenly' for δῖος. χθιζὸν ὑπηοῖον are adverbial accusatives, 'yesterday, at dawn'. ἔμβη is an unaugmented root aorist of ἐμβαίνω 'step into, embark'; νηὶ is a dative of means, 'by ship'; Πύλονδε has the directional suffix -δε. Noemon's puzzle — the same figure seen at home only yesterday, already at sea — closes his speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη πρὸς δώματα πατρός,
τοῖσιν δ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν ἀγάσσατο θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ.
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, away he went to the house of his father,
and in both of them their manly spirit was seized with wonder.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and went off to his father's house, and in both men a proud amazement seized their hearts.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη is a new closing formula (masculine), recurring verbatim at 4.715, and recorded in new-renderings.md alongside the already-fixed feminine ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασ’. θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is the table-fixed phrase 'manly spirit' / 'proud spirit' (4.548); here ἀγάσσατο, aorist middle of ἄγαμαι, is 'was seized with wonder/indignation at'.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρας δ’ ἄμυδις κάθισαν καὶ παῦσαν ἀέθλων.
sentences.l: And the suitors together they made sit down, and stopped them from their games.
sentences.i: They made the suitors sit down together and put a stop to their games.
sentences.n: κάθισαν and παῦσαν are transitive causative aorists, 'made sit, made stop', with an unnamed 'they' — Antinous and Eurymachus, resuming control of the suitors. ἄεθλον is Attic ἆθλον, 'contest, game'.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀντίνοος μετέφη Εὐπείθεος υἱός,
ἀχνύμενος·
sentences.l:
Among them then spoke Antinous, Eupeithes’ son,
grieving;
sentences.i: Among them Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke, troubled at heart;
sentences.n: A new speech-introduction formula, on the pattern of the already-fixed τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε / τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε lines but built on μετέφη, another aorist of μετάφημι 'speak among', filled with name and patronymic; recorded in new-renderings.md. ἀχνύμενος is a present participle, 'grieving, vexed'.

sentences.t:
μένεος δὲ μέγα φρένες ἀμφιμέλαιναι
πίμπλαντ’, ὄσσε δέ οἱ πυρὶ λαμπετόωντι ἐίκτην·
sentences.l:
and his heart, black all about, was greatly filled
with fury, and his two eyes were like blazing fire;
sentences.i: his heart, black through and through, swelled greatly with fury, and his eyes seemed like blazing fire;
sentences.n: μένεος is a genitive of content/cause with πίμπλαντ’, 'were filled with fury'. ἀμφιμέλαιναι, 'black on both sides', is an epithet of φρένες, the seat of feeling. ὄσσε is the dual 'the two eyes'; ἐίκτην is the dual pluperfect-with-imperfect-force of ἔοικα, agreeing with the dual subject.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ἦ μέγα ἔργον ὑπερφιάλως ἐτελέσθη
Τηλεμάχῳ ὁδὸς ἥδε·
sentences.l:
“Ah! truly a great deed has been done overweeningly —
this journey of Telemachus's;
sentences.i: “Ah, truly this journey of Telemachus's has turned out to be a great and overweening deed;
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is the table-fixed exclamation, 'Ah!' / 'Ah,'. ὑπερφιάλως is an adverb from ὑπερφίαλος 'overbearing, presumptuous'; ἐτελέσθη is an aorist passive, 'has been brought to pass'. Τηλεμάχῳ is a dative of reference/possession with ὁδὸς ἥδε, 'this journey of Telemachus's'.

sentences.t: φάμεν δέ οἱ οὐ τελέεσθαι.
sentences.l: yet we said that it would not be accomplished.
sentences.i: and yet we said it would come to nothing.
sentences.n: φάμεν is an unaugmented imperfect, 'we said, we used to say'. τελέεσθαι is the uncontracted future middle infinitive of τελέω (Attic τελεῖσθαι), in indirect statement after φάμεν, negated by οὐ.

sentences.t:
ἐκ τοσσῶνδ’ ἀέκητι νέος πάϊς οἴχεται αὔτως
νῆα ἐρυσσάμενος, κρίνας τ’ ἀνὰ δῆμον ἀρίστους.
sentences.l:
Out of so many, against our will, the young boy has gone off just like that,
having drawn a ship down, and having picked out the best men throughout the land.
sentences.i: In spite of all of us, the young boy has simply gone off, launching a ship and picking out the best men in the land.
sentences.n: ἐκ τοσσῶνδ’ ἀέκητι is 'out of so many of us, against (our) will'; ἀέκητι takes the genitive. νέος πάϊς is 'young boy', a diminishing description of Telemachus. ἐρυσσάμενος, aorist participle of ἐρύω 'draw, drag', pictures launching a ship by hauling it down the beach. κρίνας, aorist participle of κρίνω 'pick out, choose'.

sentences.t: ἄρξει καὶ προτέρω κακὸν ἔμμεναι·
sentences.l: He will go on being a source of trouble hereafter too;
sentences.i: He will go on making trouble in the future as well;
sentences.n: ἄρξει ... ἔμμεναι is future + epic infinitive (= εἶναι) of a periphrasis, literally 'he will begin to be an evil', i.e. 'this will not be the last of it'. προτέρω is a comparative adverb, 'further on, in time to come'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά οἱ αὐτῷ
Ζεὺς ὀλέσειε βίην, πρὶν ἥβης μέτρον ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l:
but for him himself
may Zeus destroy his strength, before he comes to the measure of manhood!
sentences.i: but as for him, may Zeus destroy his strength, before he ever reaches the full measure of manhood!
sentences.n: βίην, 'strength, force', is the object of the wish ὀλέσειε, an aorist optative of wish. ἥβης μέτρον ἱκέσθαι, 'to reach the measure of youth/manhood', is a fixed epic periphrasis for growing up.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι δότε νῆα θοὴν καὶ εἴκοσ’ ἑταίρους,
ὄφρα μιν αὐτὸν ἰόντα λοχήσομαι ἠδὲ φυλάξω
ἐν πορθμῷ Ἰθάκης τε Σάμοιό τε παιπαλοέσσης,
ὡς ἂν ἐπισμυγερῶς ναυτίλλεται εἵνεκα πατρός.
sentences.l:
But come, give me a swift ship and twenty companions,
so that I may lie in wait for him, for the man himself, as he goes, and watch,
in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Same,
so that most grievously he may make his voyage, for his father's sake.”
sentences.i: But come, give me a swift ship and twenty companions, so that I may lie in wait for him and watch for him as he goes, in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Same, so that he may sail to his sorrow, on his father's account.”
sentences.n: Line 669 repeats a line already published in odyssey-007, whose 'l' and 'i' are kept for that line; the rest of the sentence is new. λοχήσομαι is a future middle, 'I shall lie in wait for'; φυλάξω here is 'watch for, keep guard against'. Σάμοιο takes the familiar English form 'Same' (the Cephallenian island, distinct from Samos). παιπαλόεσσα is 'rugged, craggy'. ἐπισμυγερῶς, 'most grievously' (ἐπι- intensive + σμυγερός 'woeful'), governs ναυτίλλεται, 'sails, makes his voyage', a vivid present for a future event.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνεον ἠδ’ ἐκέλευον.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all praised it and urged him on.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all applauded and urged him on.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the table-fixed closing formula, ἔφαθ’ an elided ἔφατο. ἐπῄνεον and ἐκέλευον are unaugmented imperfects, 'were praising, were urging'.

sentences.t: αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀνστάντες ἔβαν δόμον εἰς Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l: At once then, rising up, they went into the house of Odysseus.
sentences.i: At once they rose and went into the house of Odysseus.
sentences.n: ἀνστάντες is an aorist participle of ἀνίστημι 'stand up, rise'. ἔβαν is the epic aorist of βαίνω (= ἔβησαν).

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄρα Πηνελόπεια πολὺν χρόνον ἦεν ἄπυστος
μύθων, οὓς μνηστῆρες ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βυσσοδόμευον·
sentences.l:
Nor indeed was Penelope for a long time uninformed
of the plans which the suitors were devising deep within their hearts;
sentences.i: Nor did Penelope stay long unaware of the plans the suitors were secretly hatching in their hearts;
sentences.n: ἄπυστος, 'unheard-of, uninformed', is built on the root of πυνθάνομαι 'learn by inquiry'. βυσσοδόμευον, imperfect of βυσσοδομεύω, is literally 'were building in the depths', i.e. 'were secretly devising'.

sentences.t:
κῆρυξ γάρ οἱ ἔειπε Μέδων, ὃς ἐπεύθετο βουλὰς
αὐλῆς ἐκτὸς ἐών·
sentences.l:
For the herald Medon told her, who had learned of their counsels,
being outside the courtyard;
sentences.i: For the herald Medon, who had overheard their plans while standing outside the courtyard, told her;
sentences.n: ἔειπε keeps its augment before the root's own ει-, the aorist of εἶπον. ἐπεύθετο, aorist middle of πυνθάνομαι, is 'learned of, got wind of'. ἐκτός + genitive is 'outside'.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἔνδοθι μῆτιν ὕφαινον.
sentences.l: but they within were weaving their cunning plan.
sentences.i: while they inside went on weaving their scheme.
sentences.n: ὑφαίνω 'weave' is used metaphorically of devising a plot, as of Penelope's own web later in the poem; μῆτιν here is 'a scheme, a plot'.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἀγγελέων διὰ δώματα Πηνελοπείῃ·
sentences.l: He set out to go, bringing word, through the halls, to Penelope;
sentences.i: He went to bring her the news, making his way through the house to Penelope;
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν is the table-fixed formula '(he) set out to go'. ἀγγελέων is a future participle of purpose, 'to bring word, to announce'. διὰ δώματα is 'through the halls', with διά + accusative of the space passed through.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ κατ’ οὐδοῦ βάντα προσηύδα Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: And him, as he stepped down upon the threshold, Penelope addressed:
sentences.i: And Penelope spoke to him as he stood there on the threshold:
sentences.n: A new formula, recorded in new-renderings.md: τὸν δὲ κατ’ οὐδοῦ βάντα προσηύδα Πηνελόπεια, 'and him, having come down at the threshold, Penelope addressed'. οὐδοῦ is 'threshold'; βάντα is an aorist participle agreeing with τόν, 'having stepped'. This opens the second paragraph without itself beginning one.

sentences.t: κῆρυξ, τίπτε δέ σε πρόεσαν μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί;
sentences.l: “Herald, why have the noble suitors sent you forth?
sentences.i: “Herald, why have the noble suitors sent you here?
sentences.n: μνηστῆρες ἀγαυοί is the table-fixed phrase, 'the noble suitors'. πρόεσαν, unaugmented aorist of προίημι, is 'sent forth'.

sentences.t:
ἦ εἰπέμεναι δμῳῇσιν Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο
ἔργων παύσασθαι, σφίσι δ’ αὐτοῖς δαῖτα πένεσθαι;
sentences.l:
Is it to tell the serving-women of divine Odysseus
to cease from their tasks, and for those men themselves to labour over a feast?
sentences.i: Is it to tell the serving-women of divine Odysseus to stop their work, and busy themselves instead preparing a feast for the suitors?
sentences.n: θείοιο here of Odysseus keeps 'divine', the rendering the table reserves for θεῖος (as opposed to 'heavenly' for δῖος). εἰπέμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἶπον, introducing two indirect commands, ἔργων παύσασθαι and δαῖτα πένεσθαι. σφίσι δ’ αὐτοῖς is 'for themselves', i.e. for the suitors, not the maids.

sentences.t:
μὴ μνηστεύσαντες μηδ’ ἄλλοθ’ ὁμιλήσαντες
ὕστατα καὶ πύματα νῦν ἐνθάδε δειπνήσειαν·
sentences.l:
Would that, without ever wooing, or ever again gathering elsewhere,
they might now here dine for the last and final time!
sentences.i: Would that they had never come courting, and never again gathered anywhere else, and that they were dining here now for the very last time!
sentences.n: μή ... μηδ’ with the participles and the optative δειπνήσειαν forms a wish, 'would that ... they might dine'. ὁμιλήσαντες, aorist participle of ὁμιλέω 'consort, meet together', is picked up by ἄλλοθ’ 'elsewhere, at another time'. ὕστατα καὶ πύματα doubles 'last' for emphasis, 'for the very last time'.

sentences.t:
οἳ θάμ’ ἀγειρόμενοι βίοτον κατακείρετε πολλόν,
κτῆσιν Τηλεμάχοιο δαΐφρονος·
sentences.l:
who, often gathering together, waste away much livelihood,
the substance of wise-minded Telemachus;
sentences.i: who, gathering here so often, waste away so much of his livelihood — the property of wise-minded Telemachus;
sentences.n: θάμ’ is θαμά, 'often', elided. κατακείρετε is 'cut down, consume, waste'. δαΐφρονος, 'wise-minded', keeps the fixed table rendering for the epithet, here of Telemachus rather than Odysseus, its usual bearer: a stock epithet is translated the same way wherever it lands.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι πατρῶν
ὑμετέρων τὸ πρόσθεν ἀκούετε, παῖδες ἐόντες,
οἷος Ὀδυσσεὺς ἔσκε μεθ’ ὑμετέροισι τοκεῦσιν,
sentences.i: Nor, being children, do you hear anything of what your fathers were like before you — what sort of man Odysseus was among your own parents,
sentences.n: τὸ πρόσθεν, 'formerly, in time past', with ἀκούετε used with perfect force, 'you have heard'. παῖδες ἐόντες is causal/concessive, 'seeing that you are children'. οἷος here is the rough-breathed relative 'such as, what sort of', not the smooth-breathed οἶος 'alone' seen elsewhere; the sentence runs on past the four-line mark and is cut here at the comma, since the period does not fall until 4.691.

sentences.t:
οὔτε τινὰ ῥέξας ἐξαίσιον οὔτε τι εἰπὼν
ἐν δήμῳ, ἥ τ’ ἐστὶ δίκη θείων βασιλήων·
sentences.l:
neither doing anything outrageous to any man, nor saying anything
among the people, which is the way of divine kings;
sentences.i: never doing anything outrageous to anyone, or saying a wrong word before the people, as is the way of divine kings;
sentences.n: ἐξαίσιον, 'outside the ordinary, outrageous', is the object of ῥέξας, aorist participle of ῥέζω 'do'. δίκη is 'custom, the right way'; θείων βασιλήων is 'of divine kings', θεῖος again kept 'divine' as the table reserves it.

sentences.t: ἄλλον κ’ ἐχθαίρῃσι βροτῶν, ἄλλον κε φιλοίη.
sentences.l: One man among mortals he might hate, another he might love.
sentences.i: He may hate one man and love another, as mortals do.
sentences.n: ἐχθαίρῃσι and φιλοίη are a subjunctive and an optative side by side in the same generalizing sense, 'he may hate ... he may love', a common Homeric looseness where either mood may generalize.

sentences.t: κεῖνος δ’ οὔ ποτε πάμπαν ἀτάσθαλον ἄνδρα ἐώργει.
sentences.l: But that man never at all treated any man wantonly.
sentences.i: But that man was never in any way wanton toward anyone.
sentences.n: ἐώργει is a pluperfect-with-imperfect-force of ἔοργα, perfect of ἔρδω/ῥέζω 'do'. ἀτάσθαλον here is adjectival, agreeing with ἄνδρα, 'wanton, outrageous'; the noun ἀτασθαλίαι already fixed elsewhere in the table is the related abstract noun, kept distinct from this adjectival use.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ὑμέτερος θυμὸς καὶ ἀεικέα ἔργα
φαίνεται, οὐδέ τίς ἐστι χάρις μετόπισθ’ ἐυεργέων.
sentences.l:
But your spirit, and your unseemly deeds,
are plain to see, and there is no gratitude afterward for good deeds done.”
sentences.i: But your temper and your unseemly deeds are plain for all to see, and there is no gratitude shown afterward for benefits done.”
sentences.n: ἀεικέα ἔργα, 'unseemly deeds', echoes the fixed ἀεικής already given for ἐν δόμῳ at 3.132/3.194. μετόπισθ’ is μετόπισθε, elided, 'afterward, thereafter'. ἐυεργέων is a genitive plural participle used substantivally, 'of good deeds done, of benefactions'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Μέδων πεπνυμένα εἰδώς·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed Medon, prudent counsels knowing:
sentences.i: Then Medon, a man versed in prudent counsels, spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the table-fixed reply formula, gender-adjusted for the feminine object. πεπνυμένα εἰδώς, 'prudent counsels knowing', repeats the table's fixed rendering of the fuller πεπνυμένα μήδεα εἰδώς with the noun μήδεα left understood, the same sense; this pairing with Medon by name is fixed as his own standing epithet here and at 4.711 (new-renderings.md).

sentences.t: αἲ γὰρ δή, βασίλεια, τόδε πλεῖστον κακὸν εἴη.
sentences.l: “Would that indeed, O queen, this were the greatest evil!
sentences.i: “Would that this, O queen, were the worst evil there is!
sentences.n: αἲ γὰρ δή with the optative εἴη is a wish, 'would that'. βασίλεια, vocative, 'queen', addresses Penelope directly. πλεῖστον, superlative of πολύς, 'greatest, worst', implies there is something still worse to come, as the next line shows.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ πολὺ μεῖζόν τε καὶ ἀργαλεώτερον ἄλλο
μνηστῆρες φράζονται, ὃ μὴ τελέσειε Κρονίων·
sentences.l:
But something else, much greater and more grievous,
the suitors are devising — which may the son of Cronus not bring to pass!
sentences.i: But the suitors are plotting something else, far greater and far more grievous — which I pray the son of Cronus may never bring to pass!
sentences.n: μεῖζόν τε καὶ ἀργαλεώτερον, 'greater and more grievous', comparatives. τελέσειε is an optative of wish with μή, 'may he not bring to pass'; Κρονίων is a by-form of Κρονίδης, 'the son of Cronus', i.e. Zeus.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχον μεμάασι κατακτάμεν ὀξέι χαλκῷ
οἴκαδε νισόμενον·
sentences.l:
Telemachus they are eager to kill with sharp bronze,
as he journeys homeward;
sentences.i: They are eager to kill Telemachus with sharp bronze as he makes his way home;
sentences.n: μεμάασι is a perfect with present force, 'they are eager, they are bent on'. κατακτάμεν is an aorist infinitive (= κατακτεῖναι). νισόμενον is a present participle, 'returning, on his way home'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἔβη μετὰ πατρὸς ἀκουὴν
ἐς Πύλον ἠγαθέην ἠδ’ ἐς Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν.
sentences.l:
but he had gone, in quest of news of his father,
to holy Pylos and to heavenly Lacedaemon.”
sentences.i: but he had gone in search of news of his father, to holy Pylos and to heavenly Lacedaemon.”
sentences.n: μετὰ ... ἀκουήν is 'in quest of news', μετά + accusative marking pursuit. Πύλον ἠγαθέην and Λακεδαίμονα δῖαν are the table-fixed 'holy Pylos' and 'heavenly Lacedaemon'.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τῆς δ’ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ,
δὴν δέ μιν ἀμφασίη ἐπέων λάβε·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and then her knees were loosed, and her dear heart,
and for a long time speechlessness of words seized her;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and her knees gave way at once, and her heart too, and for a long time she was struck speechless;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the table-fixed closing formula. λύτο, unaugmented aorist passive of λύω, takes γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ as a double subject, 'her knees, and her dear heart, were loosed' — the whole-and-part construction seen already at ἕρκος ὀδόντων. ἀμφασίη, 'speechlessness, being at a loss for words', governs the genitive ἐπέων.

sentences.t:
τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
δακρυόφι πλῆσθεν, θαλερὴ δέ οἱ ἔσχετο φωνή.
sentences.l:
and her two eyes
were filled with tears, and her full voice was checked.
sentences.i: and her eyes filled with tears, and her strong voice was choked.
sentences.n: δακρυόφι is an instrumental in -φι, 'with tears'; πλῆσθεν is a 3rd plural aorist passive (epic apocopated -θεν for -θησαν), 'were filled' — a plural verb with the dual subject ὄσσε, as often in Homer. θαλερή, 'blooming, vigorous', is a standing epithet of the voice or of tears elsewhere; ἔσχετο, aorist middle of ἔχω, is 'was held back, was checked'.

sentences.t: ὀψὲ δὲ δή μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβομένη προσέειπε·
sentences.l: But at last, answering him with words, she addressed him:
sentences.i: But at last she found her voice, and answered him:
sentences.n: A new formula (recorded in new-renderings.md): ὀψὲ δὲ δή μιν ἔπεσσιν ἀμειβομένη προσέειπε, 'but late indeed, answering him with words, she addressed him'. ὀψέ is 'late, at last', answering the delay just described (her seized voice).

sentences.t: κῆρυξ, τίπτε δέ μοι πάϊς οἴχεται;
sentences.l: “Herald, why has my child gone?
sentences.i: “Herald, why has my child gone off?
sentences.n: πάϊς here is the epic uncontracted nominative (= Attic παῖς). οἴχεται is present with perfect force, 'is gone, has gone', as at 4.665.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί μιν χρεὼ
νηῶν ὠκυπόρων ἐπιβαινέμεν, αἵ θ’ ἁλὸς ἵπποι
ἀνδράσι γίγνονται, περόωσι δὲ πουλὺν ἐφ’ ὑγρήν.
sentences.l:
Nor was there any need at all for him
to embark on swift-faring ships, which for men become as the sea's horses,
and cross over the vast, wet way.
sentences.i: There was no need at all for him to board swift-faring ships, which serve men as horses of the sea, and carry them across the wide waters.
sentences.n: χρεώ is an indeclinable noun, 'need', impersonal with an understood ἐστί. ἀνδράσι ... γίγνονται is the Homeric image of ships as 'the horses of the sea' for seafaring men. πουλὺν ἐφ’ ὑγρήν is πολύν, 'much, vast', with ὑγρή, 'the wet (element)', substantival for the sea.

sentences.t: ἦ ἵνα μηδ’ ὄνομ’ αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώποισι λίπηται;
sentences.l: Was it so that not even his name might be left among men?”
sentences.i: Was it so that not even his name would be left among men?”
sentences.n: ἦ ἵνα with the subjunctive λίπηται is a bitter rhetorical question, 'was it so that ...?'. μηδ’ ὄνομ’ is 'not even a/the name'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Μέδων πεπνυμένα εἰδώς·
sentences.l: Her then answered Medon, prudent counsels knowing:
sentences.i: Then Medon, a man versed in prudent counsels, answered her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is the table-fixed 'Him/Her then answered' formula. πεπνυμένα εἰδώς repeats Medon's fixed epithet from 4.696.

sentences.t:
οὐκ οἶδ’ ἤ τίς μιν θεὸς ὤρορεν, ἦε καὶ αὐτοῦ
θυμὸς ἐφωρμήθη ἴμεν ἐς Πύλον, ὄφρα πύθηται
πατρὸς ἑοῦ ἢ νόστον ἢ ὅν τινα πότμον ἐπέσπεν.
sentences.l:
“I do not know whether some god roused him,
or his own spirit itself was stirred to go to Pylos, so that he might learn,
of his own father, either his return, or whatever fate he had met.”
sentences.i: “I do not know whether some god roused him, or his own heart itself was stirred to go to Pylos, to learn of his own father — either his homecoming, or whatever fate had come upon him.”
sentences.n: ὤρορεν is unaugmented aorist of ὄρνυμι 'stir up, rouse'. ἐφωρμήθη is aorist passive of ἐφορμάω 'stir up, urge on'. πύθηται is aorist subjunctive of πυνθάνομαι, purpose. ἐπέσπεν, aorist of ἐφέπω, is idiomatic of fate, 'met with, encountered' (a doom).

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη κατὰ δῶμ’ Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l: So then having spoken, away he went, through the house of Odysseus.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and went off, away through the house of Odysseus.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἀπέβη repeats the new closing formula fixed at 4.657, here with κατά + accusative, 'down through', in place of πρός + accusative.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ ἄχος ἀμφεχύθη θυμοφθόρον, οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ ἔτλη
δίφρῳ ἐφέζεσθαι πολλῶν κατὰ οἶκον ἐόντων,
ἀλλ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ οὐδοῦ ἷζε πολυκμήτου θαλάμοιο
οἴκτρ’ ὀλοφυρομένη·
sentences.l:
And grief that destroys the spirit was poured around her, nor could she any longer
bring herself to sit upon a chair, with many men throughout the house,
but she sat down upon the threshold of her much-wrought chamber,
pitifully lamenting;
sentences.i: Soul-destroying grief poured over her, and she could no longer bring herself to sit on a chair with so many men in the house, but sat down on the threshold of her richly wrought chamber, weeping piteously;
sentences.n: ἀμφεχύθη, aorist passive of ἀμφιχέω 'pour around', has ἄχος θυμοφθόρον, 'soul-destroying grief', as its subject. ἔτλη, unaugmented aorist of τλάω, takes the infinitive, 'she could bring herself to'. πολυκμήτου, 'much-laboured-over', describes her chamber's fine workmanship.

sentences.t:
περὶ δὲ δμῳαὶ μινύριζον
πᾶσαι, ὅσαι κατὰ δώματ’ ἔσαν νέαι ἠδὲ παλαιαί.
sentences.l:
and around her all the serving-women moaned low,
as many as were throughout the house, young and old alike.
sentences.i: and all around her the serving-women, young and old alike, all who were in the house, moaned softly.
sentences.n: μινύριζον is an unaugmented imperfect, 'moaned, whimpered softly'. ὅσαι ... νέαι ἠδὲ παλαιαί is 'as many as were ... young and old', a merism for the whole household of women.

sentences.t: τῇς δ’ ἁδινὸν γοόωσα μετηύδα Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: And among them, sobbing heavily, spoke Penelope:
sentences.i: And Penelope, sobbing heavily, spoke among them:
sentences.n: A new formula (recorded in new-renderings.md): τῇς δ’ ἁδινὸν γοόωσα μετηύδα Πηνελόπεια. τῇς is the dative plural pronoun, 'to/among them', i.e. the serving-women. ἁδινόν, 'thick, close-packed', is used adverbially of weeping, 'in a thick flood of tears'. μετηύδα is imperfect of μεταυδάω 'speak among'.

sentences.t: κλῦτε, φίλαι·
sentences.l: “Hear me, friends;
sentences.i: “Listen to me, my friends;
sentences.n: κλῦτε is an aorist imperative, 'hear!'; φίλαι, vocative, addresses the serving-women as her own dear companions, not merely servants.

sentences.t:
πέρι γάρ μοι Ὀλύμπιος ἄλγε’ ἔδωκεν
ἐκ πασέων, ὅσσαι μοι ὁμοῦ τράφεν ἠδ’ ἐγένοντο·
sentences.l:
for beyond measure the Olympian has given me griefs,
beyond all the women who were born and bred along with me;
sentences.i: for the Olympian has given me griefs beyond all the women who were born and grew up with me;
sentences.n: πέρι is the adverb, 'exceedingly, beyond measure' (anastrophe, accent thrown back). ἐκ πασέων is 'beyond all', governing the partitive genitive ὅσσαι. τράφεν is unaugmented aorist passive of τρέφω, 'were reared'; ἐγένοντο is 'were born, came to be'.

sentences.t:
ἣ πρὶν μὲν πόσιν ἐσθλὸν ἀπώλεσα θυμολέοντα,
παντοίῃς ἀρετῇσι κεκασμένον ἐν Δαναοῖσιν,
ἐσθλόν, τοῦ κλέος εὐρὺ καθ’ Ἑλλάδα καὶ μέσον Ἄργος.
sentences.i: I, who first lost a noble, lion-hearted husband, a man distinguished among the Greeks by virtues of every kind, noble, whose fame spread wide through Hellas and the middle of Argos;
sentences.n: θυμολέοντα, 'lion-hearted' (θυμός + λέων), is a vivid compound epithet. κεκασμένον, perfect passive participle of καίνυμαι 'excel, surpass', takes the dative ἀρετῇσι, 'distinguished by every kind of excellence'. This whole phrase τοῦ κλέος εὐρὺ καθ’ Ἑλλάδα καὶ μέσον Ἄργος is Penelope's signature line about Odysseus, likely to recur, and is recorded as its own entry in new-renderings.md; Ἑλλάδα here is a district of Thessaly, not the whole of later Greece, and is kept as the transliterated name 'Hellas' rather than translated 'Greece'.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ παῖδ’ ἀγαπητὸν ἀνηρείψαντο θύελλαι
ἀκλέα ἐκ μεγάρων, οὐδ’ ὁρμηθέντος ἄκουσα.
sentences.l:
and now, in turn, storm-winds have snatched away my beloved child,
inglorious, out of the halls, nor did I hear of his setting out.
sentences.i: and now the storm-winds have carried off my beloved son as well, without any renown, out of the halls, and I did not even hear of his setting out.
sentences.n: ἀνηρείψαντο, aorist of ἀνερείπομαι, 'snatched up and carried off'; θύελλαι, 'storm-winds', is the subject, a mythic image for sudden, unexplained vanishing. ἀκλέα, 'without fame, unheralded', agrees with παῖδ’. ὁρμηθέντος is a genitive participle governed by ἄκουσα (a verb of perception takes the genitive of the person, here understood, with an agreeing participle): 'nor did I hear of his having set out'.

sentences.t:
σχέτλιαι, οὐδ’ ὑμεῖς περ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θέσθε ἑκάστη
ἐκ λεχέων μ’ ἀνεγεῖραι, ἐπιστάμεναι σάφα θυμῷ,
ὁππότ’ ἐκεῖνος ἔβη κοίλην ἐπὶ νῆα μέλαιναν.
sentences.l:
Cruel ones! Not even you, each one, took thought in your minds
to wake me from my bed, though you knew well in your hearts,
when that man went to the hollow black ship.
sentences.i: Cruel women! Not one of you thought to wake me from my bed, although you knew perfectly well in your hearts that he was going to the hollow black ship.
sentences.n: σχέτλιαι, vocative, 'cruel, hard-hearted ones', a reproach to the serving-women. ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θέσθε, 'put in your minds', takes ἀνεγεῖραι as its object, 'the thought to wake me'. ἐπιστάμεναι σάφα θυμῷ is concessive, 'though you knew well in heart'. κοίλην ... μέλαιναν is the table-fixed 'the hollow black ship'.

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼ πυθόμην ταύτην ὁδὸν ὁρμαίνοντα,
τῷ κε μάλ’ ἤ κεν ἔμεινε καὶ ἐσσύμενός περ ὁδοῖο,
ἤ κέ με τεθνηκυῖαν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἔλειπεν.
sentences.l:
For if I had learned that he was planning this journey,
then surely either he would have stayed, eager though he was for the road,
or else he would have left me lying dead within the halls.
sentences.i: For if I had learned that he was planning this journey, then surely he would either have stayed, for all his eagerness to be gone, or else he would have left me dead in the halls.
sentences.n: πυθόμην is an unreal-past aorist indicative in a contrary-to-fact condition with εἰ. ἔμεινε and ἔλειπεν, similarly unreal, answer each other with ἤ ... ἤ. ἐσσύμενός περ ὁδοῖο is concessive, 'eager though he was for the road', with the genitive after ἐσσύμενος. τεθνηκυῖαν, perfect participle, 'dead, having died'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά τις ὀτρηρῶς Δολίον καλέσειε γέροντα,
δμῶ’ ἐμόν, ὅν μοι δῶκε πατὴρ ἔτι δεῦρο κιούσῃ,
καί μοι κῆπον ἔχει πολυδένδρεον, ὄφρα τάχιστα
Λαέρτῃ τάδε πάντα παρεζόμενος καταλέξῃ,
sentences.l:
But let someone briskly call old Dolios,
my slave, whom my father gave me, when I was still coming here,
and who tends for me my many-treed garden, so that most quickly,
to Laertes, sitting beside him, he may recount all these things,
sentences.i: But let someone go quickly and call old Dolios, my slave, whom my father gave me when I first came here as a bride, and who tends my garden full of trees for me, so that he may go and sit beside Laertes and tell him all this as quickly as possible,
sentences.n: ὀτρηρῶς, adverb, 'briskly, promptly', echoes the table-fixed ὀτρηρὸς θεράπων 'brisk attendant'. κιούσῃ, dative present participle of κίω 'go, come', agreeing with μοι, 'to me as I came here', of Penelope's arrival as a bride. πολυδένδρεον, 'many-treed', a transparent compound describing the orchard. παρεζόμενος, present participle of παρέζομαι 'sit down beside'. The sentence continues past the four-line mark and so is cut here, at the comma that closes the purpose clause ὄφρα ... καταλέξῃ.

sentences.t:
εἰ δή πού τινα κεῖνος ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μῆτιν ὑφήνας
ἐξελθὼν λαοῖσιν ὀδύρεται, οἳ μεμάασιν
ὃν καὶ Ὀδυσσῆος φθῖσαι γόνον ἀντιθέοιο.
sentences.l:
in case that man, having woven some plan in his mind,
may go out and lament before the people, who are eager
to destroy also the offspring of godlike Odysseus.”
sentences.i: in case Laertes, weaving some plan of his own, may go out and make his complaint before the people, who are eager to destroy the offspring of godlike Odysseus as well.”
sentences.n: εἰ δή πού is 'in case, perhaps', introducing a fear-clause in sense. ὑφήνας, aorist participle of ὑφαίνω, again 'having woven', of devising a plan. ὀδύρεται is 'laments, makes complaint'; μεμάασιν, perfect with present force, 'are eager'. φθῖσαι, aorist infinitive of φθίνω 'destroy, waste away', with γόνον, 'offspring, stock'; ἀντιθέοιο keeps the table-fixed 'godlike'.
